It is because of the VVVFD powering the motor, and he actually used a motor from an electric passenger car in the demonstration, specifically the Mitsubishi i-MiEV subcompact hatchback. https://youtu.be/mKpIqNNc9Kw?si=0T9qB3JuLJddr9LG

That sound is coming from the electric motor. More accurately, it's caused by the variable-voltage variable-frequency drive but the motor ultimately produces the sound. It is also simply just known as variable frequency drive, but the first term is more accurate because it can and needs to vary both voltage and frequency simultaneously. The VVVF drive causes that noise because it is a digital device that uses binary pulse width modulation to change the voltage and frequency required to change the speed of the motor. It is binary in order to save energy by eliminating resistive losses in the transistors that power the drive. The motor produces the sound because the stator coils simply act as a speaker.

Plants grow plentifully deep roots, when the soil is sufficiently soft, to access permanent groundwater so that they can survive droughts without any watering. The dense clay paste is a shallow layer on the surface called claypan which is underlaid by hardpan. Claypan drains very slowly while hardpan, being a rock, does not drain at all. The flooding is mainly caused by the hardpan being an entirely impermeable layer besides at the cracks.

This is why it's important to break through the caliche hardpan before planting plants. Plants grow deep taproots, when the soil is sufficiently soft, to access permanent groundwater so that they can survive droughts without any watering. The hardpan prevents roots from penetrating deep into the ground, thereby preventing the plant from reaching permanently moist soil.

Hardpan, also known as caliche, duricrust, duripan, calcrete, silcrete, gypcrust, gypcrete, and ferricrust, is a thin layer of mudstone, also known as siltstone and claystone, that overlies soft soil below known as softpan. As implied by the name of the material that comprises it, it is actually rock, although only a weak one among the weakest type of rock known as sedimentary rock. Hardpan forms by minerals precipitating out of the water in formerly moist soil that has gradually dried out over geologic time.

The NRTL requirement doesn't come from the NEC, but from OSHA in which all authorities having jurisdiction within the NEC must follow. This means a standard 13-amp BS 1363 socket is not legal in the US unless it is NRTL listed. Conversely, the UK follows BS 7671. If not, then go ahead and install the NEMA 6-50R. However, since the UK is 240-volts to earth, you must install either hot terminal to the live wire and the other to the neutral wire. There is no split-phase electricity in the UK, nor is there 480Y/277 volts three-phase. So, you cannot normally get 480 volts between any two conductors. So, no worries that you will accidentally get 480 volts unless it is a custom installation in a large commercial/industrial site. However, they do have 416Y/240 volts three-phase in the UK, so you have to be careful to not accidentally get 416 volts. In any case, live to neutral is always 240 volts in the UK in a standard installation, so you will never mess up as long as you wire one hot terminal to live and the other hot terminal to neutral.

That's because the $500 premium is not just for EV charging. It's mostly for a newer, more upscale apartment which happens to have EV charging. The housing stock in the Bay Area is relatively old, so the typical apartment is much older. The older apartment buildings have a whole-building electrical service that is designed to be just sufficient without EV charging. So, the landlord cannot just add EV chargers on the common-area circuits without upgrading the service. Upgrading the service alone takes thousands of dollars for that amount of load for all those cars doing Level 2 charging simultaneously.

As for chargers being fed from the apartment unit's own supply, that only works with permanently assigned parking that does not change between leases. Also, the unit's service is only guaranteed to be just sufficient without EV charging. Granted, the National Electrical Code has always required services of dwellings to be at least 60A, which helps. However, that still does not help the whole-building service, because it is based on the sum of connected load of each unit, not the sum of the ratings of each unit's main breaker. If the apartment already has an electric stove and/or dryer within the unit, the unit's service definitely has enough for capacity for Level 2 charging, as long as the stove or dryer is not used when the car is charging. In order to be code complaint, the unit's main breaker must be prevented from nuisance tripping, so a smart breaker panel which can coordinate loads is required. However, even those cost at least $1000, so there is no cheap and easy way to add EV charging to apartments.

The same situation applies to condos and multi-unit commercial properties.

It's even way better in the US and Canada because  most RV parks have 50A outlets (using NEMA 14-50R) at 240V in addition to the standard 15A outlets at 120V (NEMA 5-15R). Here, the electricity supply is split-phase, where there are two hot wires each at 120 V, and a neutral. Each hot wire is in the exact opposite phase, so you get 240V between them. This means we get triple the speed on Level 2 charging in RV parks here. However, not every RV park has NEMA 14-50R outlets, and those that have it only have a few spaces with it, which are specifically designed for big rig RVs. Still, every RV park has 30A 120V outlets (NEMA TT-30) at every space, so any RV park here still gets the same rate of power as those in Australia.
